chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 281 to 290, Kapilar's parrot decade (கிள்ளைப் பத்து) of kurinji: every poem turns on the parrots that raid the hill millet and the girl set to drive them off. By our reading the man blesses and thanks the birds whose raids put her in the field and envies them her glance, while the friend turns the same field against him: do not come by night, your promises are a net, how can you leave her, the reaped field still holds the parrots, and the elders may end her guarding, so marry her.

281.reading: The man blesses the parrots: may they live for ages beyond counting, for they brought about the guarding of the millet by the hill girl with bright jewels, thick dark hair and broad shoulders.
281.nuance: The long-life blessing (வாழிய பலவே) that bards give kings is given to crop thieves. காவல் காட்டியவ்வே says the parrots 'showed' him her guarding: the raids that are the family's loss are his gain, since they set her alone in the field where he can see her.

thinai_evidence.note: parrots and the hill girl guarding millet, the native things of the hills

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the man is glad of what the parrots' raids gave him; no hearer is named, so he speaks aloud to no one in particular

282.reading: The friend tells the man of the land where the small parrot of the grove still waits on the big-eared millet on the slope even as the hill girl with large rain-cool eyes drives it off: do not come, the thick darkness has deepened on the forest path where tusked beasts roam.
282.nuance: The parrot that keeps eyeing the millet while the girl chases it looks like the man who keeps coming though she is guarded, but no second pair or anchor ties it to him, so it stays scene (an ullurai near miss). The refusal is for the night only; the field by day is where she can be found.

comparisons.tenor: the girl's eyes, cool and moist

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the address நாட and the command வாரல் make the friend refuse the night tryst (இரவுக்குறி மறுத்தல்)

283.reading: The friend tells the man of the land where the soft-spoken simple daughter of a hard-eyed hunter drives the green-backed small parrots from the millet sown in mixed poor soil: even if you make great promises and leave, the women caught in your net of lies are very many.
283.nuance: The opening sets the hard-eyed father against the soft-spoken daughter: she belongs to a house that can be fierce. The last line may be read as a taunt (you can leave her; you will find others in your net) or as a warning to the girl's side (many have been caught so); either way the friend names his promises as bait.

thinai_evidence.note: a hunter's daughter guarding millet from parrots

comparisons.tenor: his false promises, which trap women

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the address நாட and the reproach of his promises give the poem to the friend

284.reading: Pitiable are the red-mouthed green parrots: even seeing the long field reduced to the green-stalked stubble of millet the hill hunters have cut, they have a great love that cannot learn to part from it.
284.nuance: The whole poem is the parrots, so iraicchi fails the deletion test (strike the birds and nothing is left); the harvest that ends the girl's guard duty is what the parrots' love outlasts. Whom the pity is aimed at turns on the unstated speaker.

thinai_evidence.note: parrots, hill hunters and cut millet

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; read as the man, who like the parrots keeps returning to the reaped field where the girl no longer comes

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; or the friend, praising the birds' constancy in his hearing as a reproach and a push to marry

285.reading: The friend asks the man of the land where the hill girl with plaited dark hair and fine forehead eats soft millet flour and with her clapper drives small parrots from the hill rice: how can you bring yourself to part, leaving her here, so that her full bangles slip?
285.nuance: The friend's picture of the girl is all small domestic ease, eating millet flour and rattling the clapper; the slipping bangle (வீங்குவளை நெகிழ) is the sign of wasting that his parting would bring, so the question யாங்கு வல்லுநையோ is a charge of hardness, not a request for reasons.

thinai_evidence.note: hill girl, hill rice and parrots

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the address நாட and ஈங்கு இவள் (her, here) make the friend speak for the girl against his leaving

286.reading: The girl tells her friend that the lord of the good, ever-yielding hill, where on the white stalks of the stubble left after the small millet was cut the bean has podded and the settling parrots are driven off, seems to have loved her without blemish, yet he carries off the dark glow of her beauty.
286.nuance: His land is யாணர், yielding again even after the harvest, while her own glow is taken; போலும் (it seems) holds back from blaming him, and the loss is put on his love itself, which takes as it gives. The stubble bearing beans could be read as a hidden image of renewal, but no pair ties it to the lovers, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: millet stubble, bean and parrots of the hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the vocative தோழி and என் மாமை make the girl speak to her friend

287.reading: The friend tells the man of the land where the short-legged mountain goat on the high peak takes fright at the parrots leaping onto the millet: surely you are skilled at lying, and surely skilled at nothing else.
287.nuance: The two lines turn on one word: வல்லை (you are able) at lying, வல்லாய் (you are not able) at anything else, a sarcasm that grants him skill only in deceit. The goat startled by small birds may hint at a strong man made timid, but it does no act of the love situation, so it is scene.

thinai_evidence.note: mountain goat of the peaks and parrots in the millet

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the address நாட and the charge of lying give the poem to the friend reproaching his broken promise

288.reading: The man asks his heart what they can do in return, knowing how good it was, for the help the parrots gave: while the gentle, lovely hill girl guards the many-eared millet, they come and share it out among themselves.
288.nuance: The language of debt (செய்த உதவி, நன்று தெரிந்து, எவன் செய்குவம்) is the language of gratitude to a benefactor, put to birds who meant no help: their theft keeps her in the field. பாத்தரும் is read as share out and eat.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill girl guarding millet from parrots

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the man speaks to his heart (நெஞ்சே) during the secret love

289.reading: The friend tells the lord of the great hills that the elders, saying the parrots come to the green-eared millet on the slope because they take the hill girl's sweet voice for a parrot's, seem ready to stop even her guarding; so marry her and take her.
289.nuance: The girl's charm turns against her: her voice is so like the birds' that it calls them instead of scaring them, and that gives the household reason to take the guard from her, ending the day meetings. The accham is the girl's side's fear of the elders' command.

thinai_evidence.note: hill girl, millet and parrots in the great hills

comparisons.tenor: the girl's sweet voice, taken by the parrots for one of their own

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the address நாட and the closing வரைந்தனை கொண்மோ make the friend urge marriage (வரைவு கடாதல)

290.reading: The man says the parrots seem far more fortunate than a king of the just red sceptre devoted to right: they are looked at by the hill girl with bright, flower-fragrant hair, and they are driven off by her.
290.nuance: A comparison of excess (the ablative -இன், more than): the best a kingdom can offer is ranked below being glanced at and shooed away by her. ஒப்புதல் is the field word for driving off birds, so even her chasing is a favour he envies.

comparisons.tenor: the parrots, more fortunate than such a king

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the man, envious of the birds, speaks with no hearer named

links.note: Both count the girl's posting to the millet field as luck for the secret love: in Natrinai 134 the friend tells the girl that the mother herself sent her with the clapper to the field near the meeting place; in Ainkurunuru 281 the man blesses the parrots whose raids set her to guard.
links.teaches: Held together, the two poems show that the field watch which makes the day trysts possible is set up by agents who do not know what they serve, the mother by her order and the parrots by their raids, so the kalavu depends on the household's own ignorance.

links.note: Both refuse the night visit on the hill path: Kuruntokai 141's girl would tell him she has been sent to drive parrots from the millet and that he should not come in the deep midnight when the tiger waits; Ainkurunuru 282's friend tells him not to come in the dark where tuskers roam.
links.teaches: Ainkurunuru 282 gives only the refusal, while Kuruntokai 141 adds the alternative the refusal implies, the millet field by day, so the pair shows that the night ban in kurinji is a redirection of the tryst to the guarded field, not a denial of it.

links.note: Both turn on the man's possible lie: in Kuruntokai 25 the girl says that if he denies his word she can do nothing, since only a heron watched; in Ainkurunuru 283 the friend says that even if he makes great promises and leaves, many women are caught in his net of lies.
links.teaches: The girl of Kuruntokai 25 treats his lie as her private helplessness with no witness, while the friend of Ainkurunuru 283 recasts it as his habit, a net that has caught many, so the friend's voice turns the heroine's fear into a public charge that can be used to press him.

links.note: Both look at the reaped millet field: in Natrinai 306 the friend, in the man's hearing, says the girl has been sent home and asks how he will come day after day to the bare stubble; in Ainkurunuru 284 the parrots keep coming to the stubble, unable to part from it.
links.teaches: Natrinai 306 assumes that the harvest ends the man's reason to come, but Ainkurunuru 284 shows creatures whose love keeps them at the empty field anyway, so the harvest cannot end such a love; it only leaves marriage as the way it can go on.

links.note: Both have the friend (for Parimelazhagar in the Kural) speak to the man about to part: Kural 1151 refuses his promise of a quick return, saying tell it to those who will be alive; Ainkurunuru 285 asks how he can part and leave her here with her bangles slipping.
links.teaches: The Kural states the friend's refusal as a bare threat to the girl's life, while the Sangam poem sets the same refusal in the girl's daily field life and names the visible sign, the slipping bangle, so the Kural's abstract 'those who will be alive' is shown as wasting already begun.

links.note: Both have the girl hold to the man's goodness while her pallor spreads: in Kural 1184 she thinks of him and speaks only of his merits yet pallor comes; in Ainkurunuru 286 she says he seems to have loved her without blemish yet takes her beauty.
links.teaches: In both the girl refuses to blame the man and lays the loss elsewhere, on the pallor as a cheat in the Kural and on his love itself in the Sangam poem, so the pair shows a fixed rule of her speech: the waste of her beauty is never his fault in her own mouth.

links.note: Both use the reaped millet stubble of the hill farmer: in Kuruntokai 133 the stubble cropped by parrots puts out leaves again in the rain, as the girl lives on after his first taking of her beauty; in Ainkurunuru 286 the stubble bears pods for his ever-yielding land while her own glow is taken.
links.teaches: The same stubble is a figure of the girl's own survival in Kuruntokai 133 but of the man's endless plenty in Ainkurunuru 286, set against her fading, so the image of renewal cuts both ways: what revives on his hills need not revive in her.

links.note: Both ask what return can be made to the small parrot of the millet field: in Natrinai 194 the friend asks it of the parrot that did not take the millet ears while they played with the hill lord; in Ainkurunuru 288 the man asks it of the parrots that eat the millet while the girl guards it.
links.teaches: The parrot is thanked in one poem for eating the crop and in the other for sparing it, opposite acts earning the same gratitude, which shows that what the lovers prize is not the bird's deed but whatever keeps the field watch going and hides what they do there.

links.note: Kural 101 says that help given unasked cannot be repaid by earth and heaven together; in Ainkurunuru 288 the man, knowing the good of the parrots' help, asks his heart what he can do in return.
links.teaches: The Kural's unrepayable help is a deliberate kindness, while the parrots helped without knowing or meaning it, so the lover's echo of the gratitude maxim stretches it to an unintended benefit and makes the debt even less payable, since the helpers cannot know they are owed.

links.note: Both have the parrots take the girl's sound for their own call: in Kuruntokai 291 the man says the parrots take her clapper's sweet call for one of their own and will not rise, so she weeps; in Ainkurunuru 289 the friend says the parrots, taking her voice for a parrot's, come to the millet, so the elders may stop her guarding.
links.teaches: Kuruntokai 291 makes the image a lover's praise and a small vexation, while Ainkurunuru 289 follows it to its consequence in the household, the loss of the guard duty and so of the trysts, which turns the man's compliment into the friend's argument for marriage.

links.note: Both warn that the girl may lose the guard of the millet: in Akananuru 28 the friend, with the man nearby, warns that if she does not rise and scare the parrots her mother will send others; in Ainkurunuru 289 the friend says the elders may stop her guarding because her own voice draws the parrots.
links.teaches: The threat to the field meetings comes in Akananuru 28 from the girl's neglect, which she could mend, and in Ainkurunuru 289 from her very voice, which she cannot, so the second friend can leave the man only one remedy, to marry her.

links.note: Both have the man in love rank a small favour of the beloved above the highest good: Kural 1103 asks whether the world of the lotus-eyed god is sweeter than sleep in her soft arms; Ainkurunuru 290 says parrots merely looked at and shooed by the hill girl are more fortunate than a just king.
links.teaches: The Kural sets union against heaven, while the Sangam poem sets far less, a glance and a shooing given to birds, against a righteous kingdom, so the pair shows the measure working at both ends: even the least share of her notice outweighs the highest worldly good.

source_issues: Every colophon of the decade gives thinai only, no thurai; speakers and addressees are inferred from the poems and recorded in thurai_akam with a note.
284 has no vocative and no named hearer; whether the man or the friend speaks is a guess, and the poem's point turns on it (two alternatives recorded).
283 line 4 நீப்பினும் and line 5 பெண்டு தவப் பலவே can be construed as a taunt to the man or a warning about him; marked uncertain.
288 line 4 பாத்தரும் is read as பாத்து அருந்தும் (share out and eat); the line 2 reading follows tamilvu as shown.

289 line 1 கிளிசெத் தடுக்கத்து is read as கிளி செத்து அடுக்கத்து (taking it for a parrot, on the slope); செத்து as a likeness word is not one of the markers check accepts, so the comparison is recorded as metaphor.
